name: Esther Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you tell me goes out with your name on it. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in around half eight to our place by the bus station, an old shoe shop with six desks in it. Most of our clients are cafés, gyms and a climbing wall, and they all want social media ads every week. I'll have an AI tool spit out thirty background ideas before my coffee's cool, pick three, and then do the real work of making the type and the photos look like they belong together.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Noor, who's a care worker, and I sell risograph prints at craft fairs some weekends. Riso is a kind of old-school print machine that gives you these grainy, bright colours, I love it. The prints pay for my bus pass, basically. I've got about three weeks of money saved, which my mum thinks is terrifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I like these tools. But I'd also say good, because now the argument about paying artists whose work trained them can happen calmly. I'd post a long thread about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my edge goes. Right now I'm the fast junior because I use AI every day and the others don't. If AI stays a small helper, everyone catches up and I'm just a junior who's still not great at type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and finally take a proper typography course online, because that's my weak spot. I'd push the craft fair prints harder, maybe two fairs a month. And I'd try to get the three weeks of savings up to two months by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit deflated, a bit relieved, mostly thinking about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent. What's the pressure there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our landlord put it up twelve percent in August. My rent went up twelve percent in August, and no AI news changes the fact I've got three weeks of money in the bank. Noor works nights in a care home, so we're both stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about, even with AI as a small helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Callum, who mostly does resizing and exporting. That's exactly the routine stuff a small helper still takes. He's been there four years and he's lovely, but that's his whole day.

say: I'd admit I'm **disappointed**, because I like the tools.
I'd post about **paying artists** whose work trained the models.
think: My edge as the **fast junior** disappears if everyone catches up.
I'd be left as a junior **weak at typography**.
do: Take an online **typography course** this winter.
Sell **riso prints** at two craft fairs a month.
Build savings from **three weeks** to two months by spring.
feel: **Deflated** and **relieved** at once, with rent on my mind.
S0.quote: My rent went up twelve percent in August, and no AI news changes the fact I've got three weeks of money in the bank.
fieldNote: Her **advantage** depends on AI being useful, so a plateau **costs her**.
Her worry here is **rent**, not technology.
She's protective of a colleague whose work is **routine resizing**.

steps.text: Take an online typography course over the winter
Book two craft fairs a month to sell riso prints
Raise savings from three weeks to two months by spring
Keep using AI for ad backgrounds every day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for designers to organise, not panic. I'd say learn the tools and also demand a cut of what they make. I'd probably start a group chat for junior designers in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bits of my job I'm good at, fast drafts with AI, are exactly what the clients will do themselves. The café owner asked me last month why she needs us if she has the same app. I'm safer than the people who refuse the tools, but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward what the cafés can't do themselves: shooting proper photos of their food, planning a whole campaign, art direction. I'd ask Priya, my boss, to let me sit in on client meetings. And I'd start the junior designers' group, maybe affiliate it with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but kind of buzzing. Like the ground's moving but I can surf a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're safer but not safe. Where's the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The woman who owns the café already asked me why she needs our studio if she has the same app, and I didn't have a good answer. I'm fast, but fast isn't rare anymore in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor if your hours got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might need a third flatmate, the box room could take someone. She'd hate it, she sleeps days. But it's better than one of us moving back home.

say: I'd tell designers to **organise, not panic**.
I'd say **learn the tools** and also demand a cut of their profits.
think: My **fast AI drafts** are exactly what clients will do themselves.
I'm safer than **tool refusers**, but not safe.
do: Move into **food photography** and campaign planning for clients.
Ask Priya to let me **sit in** on client meetings.
Start a **junior designers' group** linked to the union.
feel: **Anxious** but buzzing, like trying to **surf** moving ground.
S1.quote: The woman who owns the café already asked me why she needs our studio if she has the same app, and I didn't have a good answer.
fieldNote: She sees **clients doing it themselves** as the real threat.
Her move is **up and out**: photos, campaigns, art direction.
She'd **organise** other juniors rather than act alone.

steps.text: Offer cafés food photography and full campaign plans
Ask Priya (her boss) to sit in on client meetings
Start a group chat for town junior designers, linked to the union
Advertise the box room for a third flatmate if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules and an income for everyone, fast. I'd be at protests, and I'd be online every day. I'd also say: learn what you can, because there's no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my screen work is gone by 2028, and no amount of being clever with prompts saves it. What I've got that's hands-on is the riso machine and my camera. Robots for hands-on stuff come around 2031, so that's maybe three years of print fairs and workshops, if people have money to spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the riso straight away: workshops on Saturdays, teaching people to print. I'd take any freelance photo shoots I could. I'd join every campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly. But also weirdly clear-headed, like in a fire drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if people have money to spend. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then craft fairs die first, because prints are a treat. I'd be betting on a hands-on hobby, riso printing, to pay rent in a world where nobody has spare money for prints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut, the week it became clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract down to the cheapest one, the gym, eating out, all of it. I'd probably sell my second-hand laptop and keep the old one.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules** and an **income** for everyone.
I'd tell people to **learn fast**, because there's no time.
think: My screen work is **gone by 2028**, however good I am with prompts.
**Riso and photography** give me maybe three years until robots.
do: Run **riso workshops** on Saturdays starting straight away.
feel: **Scared**, but **clear-headed** like in a fire drill.
S2.quote: I'd be betting on a hands-on hobby, riso printing, to pay rent in a world where nobody has spare money for prints.
fieldNote: She'd **pivot instantly** but knows her fallback depends on **customers' spending**.
She treats the **robot gap** as a three-year bridge, not a destination.
Progressive views turn into **basic income** campaigning.

steps.text: Run Saturday riso printing workshops for paying beginners
Take any freelance food and event photo shoots
Campaign with groups pushing for a basic income
Switch to the cheapest phone plan and quit the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's build the safety net now. I'd be pushing the union and local councillors. I'd still say use the tools while they help you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about the length of a good apprenticeship. I could build a small print studio and a photography side and have regulars by 2031. The design job goes before that, but I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for a second-hand riso machine of my own, about two thousand, over eighteen months. I'd keep the studio job and use AI to be as fast as possible there. I'd do a part-time photography course next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but motivated. Five years feels like a project, not a sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2034, when robots can do hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I think people will still pay to stand in a room with ink on their hands and a person showing them how. Maybe that's naive, but I'd bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd want to bring along with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, from the studio. He's good with machines and he'd be lost if the resizing went. We could run the print studio together.

say: I'd say use the five years to **build the safety net**.
I'd push the **union and councillors**, while still using tools that help.
think: Five years is like an **apprenticeship**: time to build a **print studio**.
My design job **ends early**, but I'd see it coming.
do: Save **two thousand** for a second-hand riso machine over eighteen months.
Keep the studio job and use **AI for speed**.
Do a part-time **photography course** next year.
S3.quote: I think people will still pay to stand in a room with ink on their hands and a person showing them how.
fieldNote: She frames five years as an **apprenticeship** for a new business.
Her bet is on **human contact**, not the craft itself.

steps.text: Save two thousand over eighteen months for a used riso machine
Use AI for every first draft at the studio
Enrol in a part-time photography course next year
Plan a shared print studio with Callum (her colleague)

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, if governments don't waste it. I'd want schools teaching kids to work alongside AI, and a fund for people whose jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually exciting. I'd have ten years to get really good, run a print studio, and probably work with AI on campaigns until 2036. Robots don't touch my riso room until 2039, and by then I'd be 40 with a name in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the studio for three or four years, learning everything I can about campaigns. I'd build the riso side slowly, a market stall first, then a rented unit. I'd keep saving, aiming for three months' cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the big picture, but personally hopeful. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound more settled here than anywhere else. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time is the thing I never have, and ten years of warning is the most time anyone has ever given me. With ten years I'd have regulars and a reputation, which a machine can't just copy overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's job, honestly, and my mum's. Care work isn't safe from robots forever, and my mum's a cashier. I'd worry about them more than me.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if **governments don't waste it**.
I'd want schools teaching kids to **work alongside AI**.
think: Ten years lets me **get good** and run a **print studio**.
Robots don't reach my **riso room** until 2039.
do: Stay at the studio **three or four years** learning campaigns.
Grow the riso side from a **market stall** to a rented unit.
feel: **Hopeful** for myself, **uneasy** about the wider world.
S4.quote: Time is the thing I never have, and ten years of warning is the most time anyone has ever given me.
fieldNote: She's the **rare junior** who feels better with AGI on a decade's timeline.
Her worry moves to **family members' jobs**, not her own.
Her plan rests on **reputation built** over years.

steps.text: Stay at the studio three or four years learning campaign work
Rent a market stall for riso prints, then a small unit
Grow savings to three months of expenses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough to build anything. What would help is a basic income while people rebuild, and cheap spaces like the old shops on the high street turned into workshops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I like the tools. I do, and I don't think that makes me a traitor to artists. I can love the AI tools and still think the people whose drawings trained them deserve to be paid.

headlineQuote: I can love the AI tools and still think the people whose drawings trained them deserve to be paid.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old junior** designer making social media ads for cafés and gyms.
She uses **AI every day** and is the fastest junior, though weak at typography.
She sells **riso prints** at craft fairs and shares a flat with a care worker.
She wants **unions** and a **basic income**, and bets on hands-on print workshops.
She's most worried by **fast AGI** and most hopeful with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** while people rebuild and cheap **workshop spaces** on the high street.
